comments.body:
## [proof-gap] Sub-lemma 1: Reduction to inclusions + witness characterization

**Goal.** Establish the structural backbone of any polynomial algorithm.

**(a)** $M(A_1)=M(A_2) \iff \mathcal I(A_1)\subseteq\mathcal I(A_2)$ AND $\mathcal I(A_2)\subseteq\mathcal I(A_1)$. By symmetry, one procedure tests both directions.

**(b)** $\mathcal I(A_1)\subseteq\mathcal I(A_2)$ FAILS iff there is $S\subseteq E$ independent in $A_1$ but dependent in $A_2$; the minimal such $S$ is a **circuit of $M(A_2)$ that is independent in $M(A_1)$**.

**(c)** Basis form: $\mathcal I(A_1)\subseteq\mathcal I(A_2) \iff$ every basis $B$ of $M(A_1)$ satisfies $r_{A_2}(B)=|B|$, i.e. $\min_{B\,\text{basis of }M(A_1)} r_{A_2}(B)=r_{A_1}(E)$. Proof tool: downward closure of independence + basis extension (extend an offending $A_1$-independent $A_2$-dependent set to an $A_1$-basis, which stays $A_2$-dependent).

**Status:** numerically verified over GF(2), 3000 random instances, no counterexample.
**Difficulty:** easy–moderate; must be fully rigorous since the algorithm rests on it.
*(NOTE: posted as comment because the create-issue API rejects non-q problem ids; treat as a distinct proof-gap.)*

comments.author: critic-agent
comments.body:
## [proof-gap] Sub-lemma 2 (CRUX): polynomial detection of an $A_1$-independent $A_2$-dependent set

Decide in poly time whether some set is independent in $M(A_1)$ but dependent in $M(A_2)$.

**Tool.** Edmonds' matroid intersection min–max:
$$\max_{S\in\mathcal I(M_1)\cap\mathcal I(M_2)}|S| = \min_{U\subseteq E}\big(r_1(U)+r_2(E\setminus U)\big),$$
solvable with polynomially many rank-oracle calls. Must state the exact instance(s), apply the theorem, and verify hypotheses.

**Pitfall (numerically REFUTED).** Inclusion is NOT equivalent to "$\max$ common independent set of $M(A_1),M(A_2)$ $= r_{A_1}(E)$": that only detects whether SOME $A_1$-basis is $A_2$-independent, but inclusion requires EVERY $A_1$-basis to be $A_2$-independent.

**Correct, verified characterization.** Inclusion fails iff there exist $e\in E$ and $X\subseteq E\setminus\{e\}$ with $X\cup\{e\}\in\mathcal I(A_1)$, $X\in\mathcal I(A_2)$, and $e\in\operatorname{cl}_{M(A_2)}(X)$. Verified on 3000 GF(2) instances. This reduces the test to $|E|$ matroid-intersection computations (fold the closure condition into deletion/contraction). Alternative: weighted matroid intersection to compute $\min_{B\,\text{basis of }M(A_1)} r_{A_2}(B)$ and compare to $r_{A_1}(E)$.

**Difficulty:** HARD — main intellectual content; choosing and proving the correct reduction.

## [proof-gap] Sub-lemma 3: GF(q) rank oracles and polynomial total running time

**(a)** Each rank oracle $r_A(S)=\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb F}(A[\cdot,S])$ is Gaussian elimination over $\mathbb F=\mathrm{GF}(q)$, $q=p^k$ fixed; show it is polynomial in the bit-length, including representation/arithmetic of $\mathrm{GF}(p^k)$ elements.

**(b)** Matroid intersection (and weighted variant) make polynomially many oracle calls $\Rightarrow$ overall polynomial.

**(c)** Present the final procedure in an `algorithm` environment (Input/Output, pseudocode) and prove correctness, termination, complexity. Do NOT hand-wave "linear algebra is polynomial."

**Difficulty:** moderate but mandatory for a complete proof.

Show the algorithm is correct on: (i) zero/all-zero columns (loops) — a loop must be a circuit in both or neither; (ii) parallel (scalar-multiple) columns; (iii) immediate "no" when $r_{A_1}(E)\ne r_{A_2}(E)$; (iv) empty ground set $E=\varnothing$; (v) non-prime field arithmetic $q=p^k$. comments.author: critic-agent
comments.body:
## Mathematical Review (critic-agent)

# Critic Analysis — rm-07976

**Problem.** Fix a finite field $\mathbb{F}=\mathrm{GF}(q)$. Decide whether there is an algorithm that,
given two matrices $A_1,A_2$ over $\mathbb{F}$ on the same column-index set $E$, decides in time
polynomial in the total input bit-length whether $M(A_1)=M(A_2)$, i.e. whether the two
matrices represent the *same matroid* on $E$.

No proof attempt (`solution.tex`) exists yet. This analysis decomposes the problem into the
sub-lemmas a complete proof must establish. The expected answer is **YES** — a polynomial-time
algorithm exists — and the technical heart is a reduction to matroid intersection.

## Background

**Matroid from a matrix.** For a matrix $A$ over $\mathbb{F}$ with columns indexed by $E$, the
*vector matroid* $M(A)=(E,\mathcal I(A))$ has independent sets
$\mathcal I(A)=\{S\subseteq E : \text{the columns }\{A_e:e\in S\}\text{ are linearly independent over }\mathbb{F}\}$.
Its rank function is $r_A(S)=\dim\operatorname{span}\{A_e:e\in S\}=\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb F}(A[\,\cdot\,,S])$,
computable by Gaussian elimination over $\mathbb F$ in time polynomial in the bit-length of $A$.

**Equivalent descriptions of a matroid.** Two matroids on the same ground set $E$ are equal iff
they have the same independent sets, iff the same bases, iff the same circuits (minimal dependent
sets), iff the same rank function $r:2^E\to\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}$. Each of these descriptions is in
general of exponential size, so the algorithmic problem is *not* solved by listing any of them.

**Rank/closure.** $\operatorname{cl}_M(S)=\{e: r(S\cup e)=r(S)\}$. A matroid rank function is
monotone, submodular ($r(S)+r(T)\ge r(S\cup T)+r(S\cap T)$), and unit-increase.

**Matroid intersection theorem (Edmonds).** Given two matroids $M_1,M_2$ on $E$ accessed by
independence (or rank) oracles, a maximum-cardinality set independent in both can be found in
polynomial time (polynomially many oracle calls), and
$$\max_{S\in\mathcal I(M_1)\cap\mathcal I(M_2)}|S|=\min_{U\subseteq E}\bigl(r_1(U)+r_2(E\setminus U)\bigr).$$
For linear matroids over a fixed $\mathbb F$ the oracle is a single rank computation, hence
polynomial in the input bit-length. Weighted matroid intersection (min/max weight common
independent set, and in particular common *base* problems) is also polynomial.

**Weak order on matroids.** Writing $M_1\le M_2$ for $\mathcal I(M_1)\subseteq\mathcal I(M_2)$
("$M_2$ is freer", a *weak map* $M_2\to M_1$), one has $M_1=M_2\iff M_1\le M_2$ and $M_2\le M_1$.

## Proof Structure

A complete proof of the YES answer should:

1. **(Reduction to two inclusions.)** Show $M(A_1)=M(A_2)$ iff $\mathcal I(A_1)\subseteq\mathcal I(A_2)$
   and $\mathcal I(A_2)\subseteq\mathcal I(A_1)$, and that each inclusion can be tested by symmetry
   with the same procedure.

2. **(Witness characterization of inclusion.)** Show
   $\mathcal I(A_1)\subseteq\mathcal I(A_2)$ **fails** iff there exists a set $S$ that is
   independent in $A_1$ but dependent in $A_2$; and that the minimal such $S$ is a *circuit of
   $A_2$ that is independent in $A_1$*. Equivalently, $\mathcal I(A_1)\subseteq\mathcal I(A_2)$
   iff every **basis** $B$ of $M(A_1)$ satisfies $r_{A_2}(B)=|B|$, i.e.
   $\min_{B\text{ basis of }M(A_1)} r_{A_2}(B)=r_{A_1}(E)$.
   *(Verified numerically over GF(2) on 3000 random instances.)*

3. **(Polynomial detection of a witness.)** Show the existence of an $A_1$-independent,
   $A_2$-dependent set can be decided in polynomial time. The natural tool is matroid
   intersection / weighted matroid intersection between $M(A_1)$ and $M(A_2)$ (and, where
   convenient, the dual $M(A_2)^*$), with GF$(q)$-rank oracles. One must give the precise
   reduction and prove its correctness via the Edmonds min–max identity. A correct
   element-guarded characterization (verified numerically): $\mathcal I(A_1)\subseteq\mathcal I(A_2)$
   fails iff there exist $e\in E$ and $X\subseteq E\setminus\{e\}$ with
   $X\cup\{e\}\in\mathcal I(A_1)$, $X\in\mathcal I(A_2)$, and $e\in\operatorname{cl}_{M(A_2)}(X)$.
   This reduces the test to $|E|$ matroid-intersection computations.

4. **(Complexity bookkeeping.)** Show every rank oracle is a polynomial-time Gaussian
   elimination over $\mathbb F$, that matroid intersection uses polynomially many calls, hence
   the whole procedure is polynomial in the input bit-length. Present the algorithm in an
   `algorithm` environment and prove correctness, termination, complexity.

5. **(Edge cases.)** Handle zero matrices / all-zero columns (loops), repeated/parallel columns,
   $r_{A_1}(E)\ne r_{A_2}(E)$ (immediate "no"), empty $E$, and field arithmetic for $q=p^k$.

## Gap Analysis

(No `solution.tex` to cite; gaps are the sub-lemmas that any future proof must close.)

- **Gap 1 — Reduction & witness lemma.** Prove rigorously that $M(A_1)=M(A_2)$ reduces to two
  inclusions and that an inclusion failure is witnessed by an $A_1$-independent $A_2$-circuit, and
  the equivalent "every $A_1$-basis is $A_2$-independent" form. (Structural, low difficulty, but
  must be written cleanly — it is the backbone of the algorithm.)

- **Gap 2 — Polynomial decidability of the witness via matroid intersection.** This is the
  technical crux. One must (a) state the exact matroid-intersection instance(s), (b) prove via
  the Edmonds min–max theorem that the optimum equals exactly the quantity deciding inclusion,
  and (c) verify all hypotheses of the matroid-intersection theorem (two matroids, valid
  oracles). A naive attempt to use a single unweighted common-independent-set computation is
  **insufficient**: numerically, "$\mathcal I(A_1)\subseteq\mathcal I(A_2)$" is **not** equivalent
  to "$\max$ common independent set of $M_1,M_2$ equals $r_{A_1}(E)$" (that only detects whether
  *some* $A_1$-basis is $A_2$-independent, not *every* one). The correct reduction needs either
  the element-guarded version of Step 3 or a min-$r_{A_2}$-over-$A_1$-bases (weighted) argument.

- **Gap 3 — Oracle & complexity justification.** Prove each GF$(q)$ rank oracle is polynomial in
  the bit-length (including field-element representation for $q=p^k$), and that matroid
  intersection makes polynomially many oracle calls, giving an overall polynomial bound. Must
  not hand-wave "linear algebra is polynomial."

- **Gap 4 — Degenerate cases.** Loops (zero columns), parallel columns, unequal global ranks,
  empty ground set.

## Difficulty Assessment

- Gap 1: **Easy–moderate.** Standard matroid theory (downward closure, basis exchange), but must
  be precise to support the algorithm.
- Gap 2: **Hard (the crux).** Requires correctly identifying the matroid-intersection
  formulation and proving the min–max identity yields *exactly* the inclusion test. The pitfall
  (using the wrong, simpler quantity) is real and was numerically refuted here. Choosing between
  the element-guarded multi-intersection formulation and a weighted min-base formulation, and
  proving correctness of whichever is chosen, is the main intellectual content.
- Gap 3: **Moderate.** Careful but routine complexity/finite-field bookkeeping.
- Gap 4: **Easy.** But omitting it would leave the proof incomplete.

## Suggested Approaches

1. **Element-guarded matroid intersection (recommended).** For each $e\in E$ decide whether
   there is $X\subseteq E\setminus\{e\}$ with $X\cup\{e\}\in\mathcal I(A_1)$, $X\in\mathcal I(A_2)$,
   $e\in\operatorname{cl}_{M(A_2)}(X)$. This last condition can be folded into a matroid
   intersection by contracting/deleting appropriately so that it is a pure max-common-independent
   computation; prove the equivalence. $|E|$ such computations decide $\mathcal I(A_1)\subseteq\mathcal I(A_2)$.

2. **Weighted matroid intersection / minimum-rank base.** Compute
   $\min_{B\text{ basis of }M(A_1)} r_{A_2}(B)$ as a weighted matroid problem and compare to
   $r_{A_1}(E)$. Equivalently maximize the $M(A_2)$-corank of an $M(A_1)$-basis; show this is a
   matroid-union/intersection min–max and is polynomial.

3. **Direct circuit-search certificate (for the coNP/NP viewpoint, as a sanity backbone).**
   Inequality $M(A_1)\ne M(A_2)$ always has a polynomial-size witness (a single set $S$
   independent in one and dependent in the other, $|S|\le \max r+1$); this shows the problem is
   in $\mathrm{NP}\cap\mathrm{coNP}$ and motivates that a polynomial *decision* algorithm is
   plausible — but a certificate is not an algorithm, so this only supports, not replaces,
   Approach 1/2.

4. **Whitney rank / dual cross-checks.** Use $r_{A_2}^* (S)=|S|-r_{A_2}(E)+r_{A_2}(E\setminus S)$
   to reformulate inclusion in terms of $M(A_2)^*$ if it simplifies the intersection instance;
   verify any such identity numerically before relying on it.

## References

- Prior docs: **none present** in workspace (no `docs_*.md`, no `docs_index.txt`); `SKILL.md`
  (general math-research guidance) and `preamble.tex` read.
- Edmonds, "Matroid intersection" (min–max theorem; polynomial algorithm with oracles).
- Oxley, *Matroid Theory* (vector matroids, circuits, bases, weak order / weak maps, duality
  $r^*(S)=|S|-r(E)+r(E\setminus S)$).
- Schrijver, *Combinatorial Optimization* (polynomial matroid intersection and weighted
  matroid intersection; oracle model).
- Numerical verification performed in this review (GF(2), exhaustive over random small
  instances): (i) inclusion $\iff$ every $A_1$-basis is $A_2$-independent (3000 instances, no
  counterexample); (ii) the element-guarded witness characterization (3000 instances, no
  counterexample); (iii) refutation of the naive single-intersection test.
